description: Curiosity's navigation camera captures the dusty Martian landscape stretching out toward distant hills in Gale Crater.
The Mastcam snaps a close-up of layered Martian rock that was once at the bottom of an ancient lake billions of years ago.
ChemCam uses a laser to zap rocks and study what they're made of. Here it targeted an interesting rock that might contain clay minerals.
Curiosity celebrates its 1,000th Martian day! The view shows the winding path the rover has taken across the crater floor.
Perseverance's very first look around after landing in Jezero Crater! You can see the flat crater floor where an ancient river delta once flowed.
Mastcam-Z zooms in on the Ingenuity helicopter sitting on the Martian surface, ready for its historic first powered flight on another planet!
A panoramic view of the ancient river delta in Jezero Crater. Billions of years ago, water flowed here and might have carried tiny living things!
SHERLOC (yes, like the detective!) uses ultraviolet light to search for organic molecules in Martian rocks. It's hunting for signs of ancient life!
One of Opportunity's last photos before a massive dust storm covered its solar panels. This brave little rover explored Mars for over 14 years!
Opportunity looks into Perseverance Valley on the rim of Endeavour Crater. The valley might have been carved by ancient water or wind.
Spirit celebrates sol 1000 at the Columbia Hills! Originally planned for just 90 sols, this tough rover kept going more than 10 times longer.
A spectacular view from the top of Husband Hill, the highest point Spirit ever reached. You can see for miles across Gusev Crater!
Curiosity takes a selfie! The Mars Hand Lens Imager on its arm can take close-up pictures of rocks AND rover selfies from multiple angles.
A Martian sunset captured by Curiosity's nav cam. Sunsets on Mars are blue because fine dust in the atmosphere scatters blue light toward the viewer!
Mastcam-Z photographs a sample tube left on the surface for future pickup. These tubes hold precious Mars rock samples that will one day be brought to Earth!
Mount Sharp towers in the background! Curiosity has been climbing this 5-kilometer-tall mountain since 2014, reading Mars's history in the rock layers.
SuperCam fires its laser at a rock from 7 meters away to figure out what minerals are inside. The zap makes the rock glow, and the camera reads the light!
